title: In Italy’s climate credit test, interest costs matter more than energy bills through 2030
summary: Italian companies’ modelled probability of default changes relatively little across the climate scenarios examined by Banca d’Italia researchers through 2030. The stricter transition paths impose some near-term pressure, but the average annual default probability in the long-term Net Zero 2050 scenario remains below 3% in 2030. It is well below the historical stress seen around Italy’s sovereign debt crisis. Much of the difference between scenarios comes through lending rates and debt-servicing costs. The direct effect of higher energy expenditure on operating earnings is smaller. The result concerns default probabilities within a six-year window. It does not show that climate risk is immaterial to the lifetime value of a bank loan or an industrial asset (Figures 8–11).

The authors link the Italian Credit Register, company financial statements, employment information and sectoral energy data. The matched sample contains roughly 904,000 limited-liability firms observed across 2013–23. Their top-down model connects energy expenditure and macroeconomic conditions to corporate operating earnings, then uses financial conditions to project firm-level default probabilities. Energy consumption cannot be read directly from every firm’s accounts, so sectoral data and estimated relationships carry information into the firm-level exercise. The researchers compare forecasts inside and outside the estimation sample and estimate separate sector models. Historical predictive performance is a check on the credit model, not evidence that it has observed an economy undergoing each of the assumed transitions (Sections 2–3, Figures 1–5).

The long-horizon NGFS pathways and the newer short-term narratives are separate sets of conditional inputs. The authors use them over a common horizon to study Italy. In the long-term pathways, early and ambitious measures can combine higher rates and weaker activity with higher energy costs. Under Current Policies, Fragmented World and Delayed Transition, the aggregate projection shows little increase in default probabilities by 2030. This ranking reflects when the assumptions bite. Chronic physical damage accumulates over a much longer period, so delaying action can look relatively benign within this window even if it produces larger long-run losses. The model comparison cannot be read as a ranking of the total economic cost of the pathways (Figures 6–10).

Alternative specifications help identify which input drives the projection. Removing interest rates from the equations brings projected default rates closer together, while varying the energy-expenditure channel by itself produces a much smaller change. Firms can partly adjust consumption, absorb costs or pass them to customers, although those choices differ by industry. Sector results show wider differences than the aggregate, including in mining and construction. For a bank concentrated in particular sectors or borrowers facing imminent refinancing, a national average is therefore a poor substitute for its own exposures (Figures 10–11, 14).

The short-term NGFS narratives also illustrate why an economically adverse event need not produce the largest credit loss within this specification: the path for policy and lending rates can offset part of a GDP shock. The authors treat the scenarios as stress-testing tools and attach no probabilities to them. They identify supply-chain and financial feedback, firm-level adaptation and more detailed treatment of physical risk as areas for improvement. Estimating bank capital impairment would additionally require exposures, recoveries and loss severity. The paper’s simulated probability of default cannot supply those quantities by itself.

questions.question: Would the limited average impact survive an actual refinancing schedule?
questions.detail: The default model is particularly sensitive to lending rates. A bank with floating-rate loans or a concentration of maturities could face a different path from the aggregate. Combine supervisory exposures and borrower debt schedules with fixed-rate shares, interest coverage and collateral recoveries. This would translate a conditional change in default probability into a more defensible portfolio loss estimate.

questions.question: Which apparently resilient sectors can pass energy costs on without losing customers?
questions.detail: The model finds a modest earnings effect on average, but historical adjustments may differ from a sustained transition in a firm with little pricing power. Match energy purchases, hedges, investment and margins with customer concentration and competitive conditions in financial statements and sector energy surveys. That would help identify where the model understates the downside for individual credits.

questions.question: How much physical and supply-chain risk lies outside the 2030 comparison?
questions.detail: The scenarios do not capture the full cumulative cost of emissions or every local disaster and inter-firm linkage. Compare longer NGFS paths with geocoded assets, insurance coverage and dependencies on vulnerable suppliers. The investment relevance is greatest for long-dated exposures whose recovery values depend on infrastructure operating beyond the model’s six-year horizon.
